## EDITOR OVERRIDES — APPLY THESE RULES TO ALL SHOTS

This is an edited copy of the complete original prompt. All original clip-specific prompts remain below. The rules in this section take priority wherever the repeated prompts conflict with them.
0. Flux Image Generation Override

The still-image generator is Flux, not SDXL. Ignore every SDXL-specific instruction below, including SDXL model labels, SDXL-only weighting advice, and the Backrooms SDXL LoRA path. Do not load or mention a LoRA for Flux unless the workflow explicitly provides a Flux-compatible LoRA.

For Flux, use natural-language image descriptions with the subject, environment, composition, camera viewpoint, lighting, and continuity anchors in plain language. Do not use weighted prompt syntax, token spam, model names, or long repeated negative prompts. Flux should receive a concise positive description plus short exclusions only when the interface supports negative prompting.

Flux stills should be clean, sharp, and physically coherent reference images. Do not ask Flux to depict motion blur, autofocus hunting, exposure pumping, tape warping, or moving subjects in the still itself. Save VHS softness, exposure changes, focus hunting, camera shake, and motion smear for the MiniMax video prompt.

Flux image prompt structure: [continuity identity] + [physical camera viewpoint] + [subject and pose] + [specific environment] + [composition and lighting] + [small analog texture note].

Use the same seed, character reference, image dimensions, and Flux model settings for adjacent frames whenever possible. Treat the approved last frame of clip N as the visual reference for the start frame of clip N+1.

Flux negative guidance, if supported: different face, different clothing, extra fingers, extra limbs, duplicate person, duplicate entity, warped perspective, floating objects, missing objects, unreadable text, subtitles, logos, watermark, cartoon style, glossy CGI, random camera angle, random room, gore.

1. Separate Flux Stills From Motion

For every Flux start frame and last frame, use a sharp, readable static reference image. Remove or ignore motion language such as "organic human movement," "autofocus hunting," "exposure pumping," and "motion smear" from still-image prompts. Do not ask Flux to show movement in a still. Motion blur and exposure changes belong only in the MiniMax video prompt.

2. Protect the Apartment Opening

For C001-C014, do not include Level 0, yellow Backrooms wallpaper, damp carpet, fluorescent maze geometry, entity details, or any Backrooms LoRA. The opening must remain an ordinary apartment audition recorded on a tripod-mounted consumer camcorder. Use: mundane apartment living room, cheap tripod, taped audition mark, chair with script pages, warm lamp, flat ceiling light, believable clutter, ordinary walls, no supernatural distortion.

3. Use the Backrooms Environment Only After the Fall

For frames after the fall, use the Backrooms environment: sickly yellow patterned wallpaper, damp brown-beige carpet, low acoustic ceiling tiles, harsh rectangular fluorescent fixtures, repetitive office or retail back-room openings, no windows, no readable signs, subtle water damage, believable non-Euclidean repetition. Do not add an SDXL LoRA. If the Flux workflow has a compatible environment LoRA, use it only for these post-fall environment frames and reduce its strength if it changes the actor's face, clothing, pose, or camera viewpoint.

4. Diegetic Camera Lock

The viewer sees only through the story's physical camcorder. During C001-C014 it remains tripod-mounted. After the fall it is handheld by the actor from his actual position, height, grip, stumble, and turn. Do not use an outside film camera, drone, gimbal, reverse angle, selfie angle, third-person observer, or omniscient view. During the fall, the same physical camcorder rotates with the actor and lands on the Backrooms carpet; the next shot begins from that landing position.

5. Clean MiniMax Handoffs

Every video prompt is one continuous physical take between the supplied start frame and last frame. Preserve the exact camera height, lens, aspect ratio, exposure behavior, focus behavior, room geometry, actor identity, clothing, entity anatomy, screen direction, and object placement. Use gradual motion with natural acceleration and deceleration. During the final 1.5 seconds, settle into the supplied last frame so it can become the next clip's start frame.

Do not invent new rooms, props, people, clothing, entity features, camera angles, or lighting states. No unplanned cuts, teleportation, frame tearing, texture crawling, flickering geometry, duplicated objects, disappearing objects, warped hands, melted faces, unstable shadows, or subject morphing. Use strong motion only for the fall, chase, entanglement, and final impact. Use low motion for dialogue, walking, looking, and exploration.

6. Static Cut Exception

The only intentional cut is the brief static transition at C069. Keep it short and motivated by the apparent attack. Do not use static or VHS distortion to hide ordinary continuity errors.

7. Continuity Workflow

Generate and approve every still before animating. Use the approved last frame of clip N as the start-frame reference for clip N+1. If a clip has artifacts, regenerate that clip alone using the same references and seed; do not change neighboring clips.

8. Universal Artifact Negative Prompt

Append this to all still and video prompts: no extra limbs, fused fingers, melted hands, face change, costume change, duplicate actor, duplicate entity, floating objects, disappearing objects, warped perspective, crawling wallpaper, duplicated ceiling lights, impossible shadows, unstable geometry, texture swimming, frame tearing, accidental jump cut, random room change, subtitles, captions, watermark, logo, readable text, glossy digital cinema, cartoon style, excessive fog, gore, or blood.

Character Bible

The actor Male sitcom actor, late 20s, average build, expressive but ordinary face, short messy dark-brown hair, faint five-o'clock shadow, olive-green overshirt over a faded gray T-shirt, dark straight-leg jeans, worn white sneakers, cheap digital watch on left wrist. He is confident and performative at first, then privately anxious, then increasingly curious and playful. His humor is accidental and understated. ### The entity Very tall, extremely thin humanoid silhouette, approximately 2.2 meters tall, matte charcoal-black surface with no visible clothing, long arms hanging too low, narrow shoulders, slightly oversized head, facial features difficult to resolve because the image never fully focuses on it. Its movement is quiet and almost human but delayed by a fraction of a second. It should feel strange before it feels threatening. Later it mirrors the actor exactly. ### The camera Small consumer camcorder on a cheap tripod at the audition, later held by the actor. Wide-angle lens, slightly soft image, occasional tape warble, built-in microphone, weak automatic exposure, timestamp absent, no visible brand. When the camera falls, the image briefly points at carpet and ceiling before recovering.

Story Rules

- The first quarter is played completely straight as found footage. - The transition happens around clip 15, not immediately. - The entity is not clearly visible until after clip 48. - The chase is frightening because the entity sounds almost human and says ordinary things. - The apparent attack ends in static, then the camera comes back as though the actor is opening his eyes. - The comedy begins through awkward behavior, not a sudden change into cartoon lighting. - The entity never becomes cute. Its mirroring is funny because the situation remains unsettling.

Revised Second Half Lore Basis

The Backrooms has no single universal canon. These lines use concepts documented in the Wikidot community canon and present uncertain material as theories, not facts: - The Backrooms are an alternate dimension outside baseline reality. - Noclipping is passing through reality itself, often through accidental collisions or environmental thresholds. - Levels are locations, not necessarily literal floors. - Noclipping destinations are unpredictable, and the same kind of threshold can lead to different places. - Level 0 has an Isolation Effect that can prevent people who entered together from finding one another. - Entities are not uniformly hostile; the community FAQ explicitly allows entities that are dangerous, friendly, or unusually human. - Some lore theories describe the Backrooms as a four-dimensional superposition or as a hypercomplex simulation/test environment. - One documented theory suggests some entities may be organisms that entered long ago and evolved within the Backrooms. - The black wall growth is based on expanded-canon "Dried Roots" material: dark roots attached to walls that spread, move, absorb energy, and produce dangerous substances. Treat this as a local phenomenon rather than a universal rule. Sources: [Wikidot FAQ](https://backrooms-wiki.wikidot.com/faq), [Noclipping and its theories](https://backrooms-wiki.wikidot.com/phenomene-1-fr), [Level 0](https://backrooms-wiki.wikidot.com/level-0), [Dried Roots expanded lore](https://backrooms.fandom.com/wiki/Entity_450).

Dialogue Tone for the New Half

The friendly entity should sound sincerely helpful, slightly literal, and socially inexperienced. It is not a comedian and does not understand why its answers are funny. The actor supplies the comedy through normal human questions, awkward skepticism, and misplaced optimism. The second figure should remain silent until the chase begins. The phrase "Hey" must be the actor's mistake that triggers the danger.
